reason:
Every measurement in the finding reproduces exactly, on both grounds, and it is still refuted on scope and on the fix. WHAT IS TRUE. Driven at 1440x960, v=paper and v=ink, owner-flight: open Menu tasting at The Orchard, press Hidden, press Done -> .b-undo data-empty="false", .b-undoText = "Menu tasting at The Orchard is now hidden from guests.", .b-undoAct enabled, .b-field[data-undo="true"], record.hidden written to the fixture. Press Preview -> data-state=desk, the guest sees 6 items not 7 (the hide carried). Press Back to the plan -> data-state=owner-flight, the moment is still data-visibility="hidden", and .b-undo is data-empty="true", .b-undoAct.disabled=true, data-undo gone, Ctrl+Z inert. Identical through the Publish round trip and identical on ink. I also drove the sharpest case the finding does not name: delete Send the invitations, Preview, Back -> the record is gone from F.milestones for good and no control in the product can bring it back (0 page errors). So the mechanism is real and reported honestly.

WHY IT IS REFUTED. (1) It is the lab's mount model, not a decision anyone made about undo. history.length = 0 sits inside render(state) (render-b.js:2034), and render(state) is reached by exactly one path: __elevate.setState + __elevate.mount (render-core.js). go() calls it, and so does the console's chooser -- console.shell.html:296-298 calls api.setState(current.state) then api.mount() on EVERY change, including the ground toggle, the width, past and accent. Flipping paper to ink remounts. So the clear is the guard that stops an operator clicking through fourteen states, or flipping the ground, from carrying undo entries whose closures point at nodes destroyed three remounts ago -- and it is load-bearing for the harness, not for the product. Preview is wired onto that same state list: it lands on "desk", one of the fourteen captioned lab states, with its own caption ("Received - desk width") and its own frame in shots/. The round trip is a lab state jump that a product control happens to trigger, which is the ground the brief names.

(2) The offer is withdrawn honestly, so the lesson it invokes is not breached. "Never destroy the control that would undo it" is the DEAD-END FILTERS bullet in lessons.md -- a filter hiding the row that carries a still-valid undo. Here the bar empties, the button disables and tabindex goes to -1: no dead control, no lie, no live offer that reverses nothing. That is the exact failure round 2 fixed ("a delete left a live offer to restore a row that no longer existed"), and this is the safe side of it. The applicable lesson, "Nothing reversible," is satisfied -- one reversibility surface, a keyboard binding, a place it lives.

(3) "The change cannot be reversed after returning" is false for five of the six grammars. Measured: after the round trip, re-opening the moment and pressing Shown reverses the hide in the same two gestures that made it AND refills the bar ("Menu tasting at The Orchard is now shown to guests."). Move, rename, hide, show and add are all re-doable through the same editor. Only delete is genuinely one-way, and previewing between a delete and the undo you meant to press is not "the owner's most ordinary loop" -- the ordinary loop is hide, rename, move.

(4) The fix is implementation plumbing with nothing visible in it. Re-resolvable entries, reversals stored as data, scoping the clear to a fresh load, a paintUndo after mount -- not one pixel, one string or one gesture changes. It is a state-storage question, and the data model is out of scope for this engagement. Applied here it would also make the harness worse: undo would survive a ground flip and a chooser jump into print or unfurl, which is what history.length = 0 exists to prevent.

(5) The only fix that would show on screen -- telling the returning owner their undo was spent -- makes it worse: a notice on arrival back at the plan, printed on every return, for a reversal the owner almost never wanted. It does not restate a gate (interaction-check.mjs:1279 proves the PLAN survives, deliberately not the stack), and the finding is right that automation does not see it. It is still a note about how a prototype stores state, not a defect in the design at a 9.5 bar.
